newsitem.title: UK: Santa Fe sale puts focus on Kuwait oil restructure.
newsitem.headline: Santa Fe sale puts focus on Kuwait oil restructure.

text.p: Kuwait Petroleum Corp may shed further assets after a $1.23 billion sale of a North Sea unit provided it can agree with its political masters the priorities and timing of its ambitious restructuring, oil analysts say.

The sale to Norway's Saga of North Sea explorer Santa Fe Exploration, announced on Wednesday, is part of a multibillion dollar strategy aimed at refocussing the Kuwaiti conglomerate on its core activity of producing and refining.
A likely candidate for sale in the next two years could be Kuwait Foreign Petroleum and Exploration Company, which after 16 years of operation is finally making profits, some oil officials say.
"KUFPEC's projected profits are precisely why it is a good time to sell. We could get a very good price," a Kuwaiti oilman said.
A growing proportion of KUFPEC's revenue is expected to come from its share of the offshore Yacheng gas field in the South China Sea.
But questions remain over the timing of the overall restructuring.

Analysts impressed by the rapid repair of the oilfields following the 1991 Gulf War, are surprised at the relaxed pace of the further development of an industry that accounts for 85 percent of Kuwait's export earnings and almost half of gross domestic product.

"It would definitely be good for the Kuwaiti economy if KPC were to start implementing strategy for increasing production capacity," said Randa Azzar, chief economist at National Bank of Kuwait. "The increase would definitely give the other sectors a boost."

The plan has an importance far beyond the oil industry for officials acknolwedge Kuwait's oil-funded investments were a factor in helping fund and assemble the Gulf War army that ended Iraq's occupation.

The restructuring includes shedding assets seen as incompatible with KPC's core functions such as expanding crude and refining capacity, upgrading refineries, expanding its oil tanker fleet, launching mainstream petrochemical output and privatising domestic petrol stations.
Domestic refinery upgrades, investment in joint venture Indian oil refineries and an aggressively pursued petrochemical project involving Union Carbide are all in the works.

But there has been little apparent progress on expanding secondary recovery in the giant but ageing oilfields containing 10 percent of global reserves. Western oil experts said that work will be needed in the next decade simply to maintain current crude production, let alone expand it.

Althougn KPC is flush with cash, government officals are cautious, questioning whether Kuwait, forbidden by OPEC from producing over two million barrels per day (bpd), should expand crude capacity just yet.

There is also political uncertainty, since Western oil majors which would provide the technology are seeking a return in the shape of involvement by way of equity or service fees in crude oil production.

"We are still waiting. We have been waiting for a long time (to get the government go ahead)," sighed one senior oilman who has watched uncomfortably as projects which require lead times of many years languish in government in-trays.
Other parts of the timetable also look under pressure -- in particular planned expansion of crude output capacity to 3.0 million bpd by the year 2000 and to 3.5 million bpd by 2005.
The problem is not money in itself -- KPC can call on general reserves and provisions for replacement of fixed assets of up to about $10 billion.

But some officials are concerned that if the govenrment does not allow it to start using its cash pile soon, spending pressure in other sectors of the economy could tempt the government to draw on some KPC reserves.

Some oil officials privately express frustration that Kuwait has had five oil ministers since the Gulf crisis, turning the job into a political revolving door that has diminished the clout of the oil sector at the highest levels of government.

It is a far cry from the 1980s when KPC was chaired by the forceful former oil minister Sheikh Ali Khalifa al-Sabah, a dynamic oil industry specialist and member of the ruling family who was given a free hand to expand KPC into an integrated oil major with a worldwide presence.
